turn_text: That's a good question. I'll just give a couple of examples. In the house, I tried to kind of cut my teeth on issues of spending or limited government. And at that time, there was a practice called earmarking, which was particularly insidious. And my party, the Republican Party, was in charge of both chambers. for much of my time in the house, and my party was guilty of some egregious abuses of spending, not just overspending, but the type of spending that became corrupting when members of Congress had the ability to basically take lots of money and distribute it however they wanted to. And on that, I went over a series of years in the house, went to the house floor again and again and again to try to cut out this type of spending in ways that my leadership in the Republican Party couldn't stop me. And there were times I went after the speaker in my own party for some of these abuses. That didn't make me very popular for a time. And that was something I felt that I couldn't compromise on. This was a practice that needed to go. And it took a while. It took several years, but ultimately, after a few of my colleagues actually went to jail for abuses relating to earmarks. And after everybody just became disgusted with the process, we abandoned earmarks. We got rid of them completely. And so, but that one was one that I felt I couldn't compromise on. On other things, on immigration, I've tried for 18 years to get an immigration package through the House and the Senate. I've introduced several pieces of legislation that the furthest we've got was in the Senate in 2013 where we have what was called the group or the gang of eight for Democrats, for Republicans, and produced a big bill that in the end had a lot of things that I didn't like in it. But a lot of things that I did as well, and it was the nature of compromise that's in particular how the Senate works. The Senate is not a majoritarian institution. One party can block even if they're in the minority because of the filibuster, which is a good thing, can block the majority from having its will. And so you learn to compromise, particularly in the Senate. Barry Goldwater, who was one of my political idols from the state of Arizona, everybody knows him as kind of this unbending conservative who went to the convention in 64 and said, you know, moderation in pursuit of justices, no virtue, and extremism, you know, that is a good thing basically, he said. But he also said later in his life, He said, politics is nothing more than public business. Sometimes you make the best of a mixed bargain. And when you're in politics long enough, you understand that politics is the art of compromise. And there are some things that you simply have to compromise because you can't impose your will. And that's generally a good thing. So some things that are kind of moral issues or issues that there are bigger things at play, maybe you don't want to compromise on, but there are things that you simply say, I want legislation passed, I'm going to have to have the meeting of minds and you have to compromise. So it's a lot of both and you kind of see it when you get there.
